chapter: The Savoy band and the Swing era
title: No identifiable Benny Carter sound or gimmick
summary: He says none of his bands had an identifiable sound the way Goodman's or Miller's did.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Big band discipline versus small-group freedom

blocks.x: This band -- did you have some particular motive and style of music that you wanted to get played with this band that forms in '32 and '33 and which Teddy Wilson joins?

No. I don't think I did, and I think that had another thing, maybe - had something else to do with the band not becoming a great commercial success. I don't think any band I ever had had a really identifiable Benny Carter sound. You know, like ... I think the Goodman band developed that and of course, the Glenn Miller Band,
which was not really a swing or a jazz band. They had that by virtue of the sound of the clarinet lead thing and certain other things. But I don't know; maybe ...

Of course, it was not until about '34 or '35, wasn't it -- that all these bands kept coming up with rippling rhythm and all these things, because there were so many of them that they had to have something ...
But in the early 30's or late 20's -- let's say, did Duke have some gimmick like that? I don't remember any.
Well, I think Duke has always had a sound, but without a gimmick, you know?
Yes. Well, I think a lot of people would say that your bands have always had a sound.
Oh, I think so. But again, without a gimmick.

I mean it was not something like that, and it seems that for a popular success though, which is what we're talking about now, it seems you have to have some identifiable quality. People like to be able to recognize
